prompt: Design OAuth for a native public client using authorization code flow, PKCE S256, exact redirects, one-time state/code handling, refresh rotation, and resource-server audience/scope validation.
Review OpenID Connect login for issuer/discovery/JWKS binding, ID token signature/algorithm/audience/time/nonce validation, and strict separation between ID tokens and API access tokens.
Fix OIDC mix-up risk for a client using multiple identity providers by binding each response to the expected issuer and client session and validating metadata and keys for that issuer.
Harden an authorization code flow with exact URI matching, PKCE, state correlation, one-time code redemption, downgrade rejection, and token/code leakage controls.
Use DPoP to sender-constrain a high-risk public OAuth client, including proof JWT validation, access/refresh token binding, replay handling, audience restriction, and compromise response.
Design local password, passkey, MFA, recovery, authenticator replacement, throttling, and reauthentication policy; no OAuth or federation flow is involved.
Define tenant/object/field/action permissions after the user identity is already established and tokens are validated; delegated protocol mechanics are unchanged.
Review CSP, XSS, CSRF, CORS, cookie, framing, and postMessage behavior for a browser application that does not participate in a federation flow.
Design KMS/HSM generation, rotation, envelope wrapping, access policy, audit, backup, and destruction for service signing keys; token protocol behavior is not changing.
Execute the existing OAuth/OIDC security test suite and issue the control verdict for redirects, PKCE, issuer, nonce, audience, and refresh replay; the protocol design is already fixed.
The product uses OpenID Connect plus local passkey step-up. Keep the OIDC issuer/token/nonce/redirect flow in oauth-oidc and the local passkey authenticator lifecycle in secure-authentication.

The API accepts OAuth tokens and enforces tenant policy. OAuth/OIDC owns issuer, audience, scopes, and token binding; authorization-security still decides whether that subject may touch the requested resource.

The browser client needs an authorization code flow plus wider browser protections. OAuth/OIDC owns redirects, PKCE, state/nonce, issuer/token checks, and token handling; web-security owns CSP/CORS/cookies and other origin defenses.
